spatial_claims.claim: Triangles ABC and DCB are congruent by SAS (AB=DC, BC=CB, angle ABC=angle DCB), giving AC=DB
Triangle BCD is isosceles (BC=CD), so angle DBC = angle BDC = mu; and angle BCA = mu from Step 3 correspondence
Angle decomposition at C: angle BCD = angle BCA + angle ACD, so ray CA lies between rays CB and CD at vertex C
Angle decomposition at B: angle ABC = angle ABD + angle DBC, so ray BD lies between rays BA and BC at vertex B
Triangles ACD and BDA congruent by SAS (AC=BD, CD=BA, angle ACD=angle DBA), giving angle CDA = angle BAD
Triangle ADE is isosceles (DE=EA), so angle DAE = angle ADE
Angle decomposition at D: angle CDE = angle CDA + angle ADE, so ray DA lies between rays DC and DE at vertex D
Angle decomposition at A: angle EAB = angle EAD + angle DAB, so ray AD lies between rays AE and AB at vertex A
Triangles BCD and CDE congruent by SAS (BC=CD, CD=DE, angle BCD=angle CDE), giving BD=CE; combined with AC=BD gives AC=BD=CE
Angle decomposition at C: angle BCD = angle BCE + angle ECD, so ray CE lies between rays CB and CD at vertex C
Triangles ABD and BCE congruent by SAS (AB=BC, BD=CE, angle ABD=angle BCE), giving AD=BE
Triangles ADE and BEA congruent by SSS (AD=BE, DE=AB, EA common), giving angle DEA = angle EAB
Triangles EAB and EDC congruent by SAS (EA=ED, AB=DC, angle EAB=angle EDC), giving EB=EC and angle ABE=angle DCE
Triangle BEC is isosceles (EB=EC), so angle EBC = angle ECB
Angle decomposition at C: angle BCD = angle BCE + angle ECD, so ray CE lies between rays CB and CD at vertex C
Angle decomposition at B: angle ABC = angle ABE + angle EBC, so ray BE lies between rays BA and BC at vertex B
Triangles EAB and BCD congruent by SAS (EA=BC, AB=CD, angle EAB=angle BCD), giving EB=BD
Triangles BCD and DEA congruent by SAS (BC=DE, CD=EA, angle BCD=angle DEA), giving BD=DA
Triangle BDA is isosceles (BD=DA), so angle ABD = angle BAD
Triangle BCD is isosceles (BC=CD), so angle DBC = angle BDC
From BCD congruent to DEA correspondence, angle BDC = angle DAE
Angle decomposition at B: angle ABC = angle ABD + angle DBC, so ray BD lies between rays BA and BC at vertex B
Angle decomposition at A: angle EAB = angle DAB + angle DAE, so ray AD lies between rays AE and AB at vertex A

configuration_map: Pentagon ABCDE is equilateral (all sides equal) and implicitly convex. Vertices are in cyclic order A-B-C-D-E. Key diagonals and their spatial positions: (1) Diagonal AC connects A to C, passing through the pentagon interior. At vertex C, ray CA lies inside angle BCD; at vertex A, ray AC lies inside angle EAB. (2) Diagonal BD connects B to D, passing through the interior. At vertex B, ray BD lies inside angle ABC; at vertex D, ray DB lies inside angle CDE. (3) Diagonal DA connects D to A through the interior. At vertex D, ray DA lies inside angle CDE; at vertex A, ray AD lies inside angle EAB. (4) Diagonal CE connects C to E through the interior. At vertex C, ray CE lies inside angle BCD. (5) Diagonal BE connects B to E through the interior. At vertex B, ray BE lies inside angle ABC. (6) Diagonal EB connects E to B through the interior (used in Case II). All diagonals of a convex pentagon pass through its interior and enter the interior of the angles at both endpoints, making all claimed angle decompositions geometrically valid. No point changes position across steps; all diagonal positions are mutually consistent.
pass_reason: All spatial claims are mutually consistent for a convex equilateral pentagon. The proof makes extensive use of angle decompositions by diagonals (AC, BD, DA, CE, BE), and in every case the diagonal passes through the pentagon interior, correctly entering the interior of the relevant angle at the vertex. Triangle congruences are properly set up with correct side-angle correspondences. No point is placed in contradictory positions across different steps, and no angle decomposition conflicts with any other. The proof handles both consecutive and non-consecutive cases with consistent geometry throughout.
